items.q: (A) No sooner the bell had rung (B) than the pupils streamed out of the laboratory, (C) leaving their unfinished experiments (D) to be cleared away by the technician.
options: No sooner the bell had rung
than the pupils streamed out of the laboratory,
to be cleared away by the technician
items.correction: No sooner had the bell rung
items.explanation: A negative adverbial such as No sooner at the start of a clause forces subject–auxiliary inversion: No sooner had the bell rung than…

items.q: The coach (A) insisted that every player (B) attends the extra session on Saturday, (C) however tired they might feel after (D) such a punishing week.
options: attends the extra session on Saturday,
however tired they might feel after
items.correction: attend the extra session on Saturday,
items.explanation: After verbs of demand such as insist that, the that-clause takes the base-form subjunctive: insisted that every player attend.

items.q: (A) Walked along the cliff path, (B) we watched the lighthouse come into view, (C) its white tower (D) gleaming against the grey sky.
options: we watched the lighthouse come into view,
items.explanation: The subject we performs the action of walking, so the participle clause must be active: Walking along the cliff path. The past participle Walked would make the clause passive, as if someone had walked us.

items.q: (A) Had the architect (B) taken the soil survey seriously, the tower (C) would not now be leaning (D) so alarming towards the canal.
options: taken the soil survey seriously, the tower
items.explanation: The word modifies the verb leaning, so it must be an adverb (alarmingly), not the adjective alarming.

items.q: If my grandmother (A) had not emigrated in 1962, (B) she says, (C) she will still be living in a village (D) where nobody owned a car.
options: she will still be living in a village
items.correction: she would still be living in a village
items.explanation: This is a mixed conditional (past condition, present result): the result clause takes would + be + -ing, never will.

items.q: (A) Bitterly cold winds (B) swept across the plateau, (C) making it highly improbable that the expedition (D) could reach its deadline.
options: making it highly improbable that the expedition
items.explanation: The collocation is meet a deadline; you reach a place or a total, but you meet or miss a deadline.

items.q: (A) Every autumn my father (B) wishes he can (C) still climb the ridge behind our village (D) as easily as he once did.
options: still climb the ridge behind our village
as easily as he once did
items.explanation: A wish about a present ability that is unreal takes the past form: wishes he could, not can.

items.q: (A) It was not until the final whistle when (B) the home supporters (C) realised how narrowly their team (D) had escaped relegation.
options: It was not until the final whistle when
items.correction: It was not until the final whistle that
items.explanation: A cleft sentence with It was not until … is completed by that, not when: It was not until the final whistle that they realised.

items.q: The chef (A) admitted that (B) he had added (C) too many saffron to the risotto, (D) which explained its bitter aftertaste.
options: too many saffron to the risotto,
items.correction: too much saffron to the risotto,
items.explanation: Saffron is an uncountable noun, so it takes too much; too many is only used with plural countable nouns.

items.q: The documentary (A) about deep-sea vents (B) was so gripping (C) that even my restless cousin (D) sat through it in so complete silence.
options: sat through it in so complete silence
items.correction: sat through it in such complete silence
items.explanation: Before an adjective + noun phrase (complete silence) the intensifier is such; so is used only before a bare adjective or adverb.

items.q: Scarcely (A) had the snow stopped (B) that the neighbours (C) were out with shovels, (D) clearing a path to the bus stop.
options: clearing a path to the bus stop
items.explanation: The pattern is Scarcely/Hardly had … when; than belongs only to No sooner, and that fits neither.

items.q: (A) My sister thrives on the pressure of live performance, (B) whereas I prefer the quiet of the practice room, (C) despite we play (D) the very same instrument.
options: My sister thrives on the pressure of live performance,
whereas I prefer the quiet of the practice room,
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and cannot introduce a clause with a subject and verb; a clause needs the conjunction although or even though.

items.q: (A) Although the heavy investment in new turbines, (B) the island still (C) relies on diesel generators (D) whenever the wind drops for more than a day.
options: Although the heavy investment in new turbines,
whenever the wind drops for more than a day
items.correction: Despite the heavy investment in new turbines,
items.explanation: Although is a conjunction and must be followed by a clause; before a noun phrase (the heavy investment) the preposition Despite or In spite of is required.

items.q: The national scholarship (A) rewards students who (B) read widely, (C) argue persuasively and (D) writing with precision under pressure.
items.explanation: Items in a list must be parallel: read, argue and write are all finite verbs, so the -ing form breaks the parallelism.

items.q: Not only (A) did the storm flatten the orchard, (B) but also it (C) tore the roof off the barn (D) where the harvest had been stored.
options: did the storm flatten the orchard,
tore the roof off the barn
where the harvest had been stored
items.explanation: In the correlative not only … but also, when the second clause has its own subject, also goes after the subject: but it also tore.

items.q: The residents (A) demanded that the council (B) publish the noise data and (C) that the airport was fined (D) for every night-time landing.
items.explanation: Both that-clauses after demanded take the subjunctive; the passive subjunctive is be + past participle (be fined), matching publish in the first clause.

items.q: (A) Been abandoned for decades, (B) the mill on the river (C) has become (D) a nesting site for herons and kingfishers.
options: a nesting site for herons and kingfishers
items.explanation: A passive participle clause begins with the past participle alone (Abandoned) or with Having been abandoned; Been can never stand on its own.

items.q: Under no circumstances (A) should a diver (B) ascends faster than (C) the rate printed on the table, (D) however calm the water appears.
options: the rate printed on the table,
items.explanation: Even when the subject is inverted after Under no circumstances, the verb after the modal should stays in the bare infinitive: should a diver ascend.

items.q: The physicist (A) whose lecture we attended (B) last spring (C) has since been awarded a prize (D) of which few of her colleagues expected.
options: has since been awarded a prize
of which few of her colleagues expected
items.correction: which few of her colleagues expected
items.explanation: Expect takes a direct object, so the relative pronoun is simply which (or that); the preposition of has nothing to attach to.

items.q: The guide (A) warned us (B) the previous evening that (C) the pass will be impassable (D) if the wind shifted to the north overnight.
options: if the wind shifted to the north overnight
items.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb (warned), will shifts back to would, matching the past shifted in the if-clause.

items.q: (A) The more remoter the village, (B) the harder it is (C) to persuade young doctors (D) to take up a post there.
options: to take up a post there
items.explanation: A comparative is formed either with more or with -er, never both; remote takes more remote.

items.q: (A) Despite his reputation for arrogance, (B) the conductor proved (C) remarkably receptive of (D) suggestions from the youngest players.
items.explanation: The adjective receptive collocates with the preposition to: receptive to suggestions.

items.q: (A) Although dial-up connections seem laughably slow today, (B) in 1990s they (C) opened the door to a world (D) most families had never glimpsed.
options: Although dial-up connections seem laughably slow today,
opened the door to a world
items.explanation: A decade written as a plural number always takes the definite article: in the 1990s.

items.q: (A) Neither the recipe (B) nor the notes (C) scribbled in the margin (D) explains why the dough must rest overnight.
options: explains why the dough must rest overnight
items.correction: explain why the dough must rest overnight
items.explanation: With neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject; the notes is plural, so the verb is explain.

items.q: The head teacher (A) asked that the matter (B) be kept strictly (C) between she and me (D) until the governors had met.
items.explanation: After a preposition such as between, every pronoun takes the object form: between her and me.

items.q: By the time the rescue helicopter arrived, (A) the climbers were sheltering (B) under the same overhang (C) for nearly nine hours (D) with hardly any water.
items.explanation: An action continuing up to a past moment (by the time … arrived) over a stated duration (for nine hours) needs the past perfect continuous.

items.q: Nobody in the audience (A) could work out (B) how had the magician (C) swapped the envelopes (D) while both his hands were visibly empty.
options: while both his hands were visibly empty
items.explanation: An embedded question keeps statement word order: work out how the magician had swapped, with no inversion after how.

items.q: (A) Hardly the paint had dried (B) on the new mural when (C) a passing lorry (D) sprayed it with mud from the gutter.
options: sprayed it with mud from the gutter
items.explanation: When Hardly opens the sentence, the auxiliary moves before the subject: Hardly had the paint dried when…

items.q: The archivist (A) warned that (B) a great deal of the letters (C) had been damaged by damp (D) long before the collection was catalogued.
options: a great deal of the letters
long before the collection was catalogued
items.correction: a great many of the letters
items.explanation: A great deal of is used only with uncountable nouns; with a plural countable noun like letters the quantifier is a great many of or many of.

items.q: (A) Newcomers to the plateau (B) struggle to sleep for the first few nights (C) because it has so a thin atmosphere (D) that even walking leaves them breathless.
options: struggle to sleep for the first few nights
because it has so a thin atmosphere
that even walking leaves them breathless
items.correction: because it has such a thin atmosphere
items.explanation: With a/an + adjective + noun the intensifier is such (such a thin atmosphere); so would only work in the order so thin an atmosphere.

items.q: (A) If the dam had been built (B) ten kilometres further upstream, (C) the old town (D) will still be standing on its original site today.
options: If the dam had been built
will still be standing on its original site today
items.correction: would still be standing on its original site today
items.explanation: A past unreal condition with a present result is a mixed conditional; the result clause needs would, and will is impossible after an unreal past-perfect if-clause.

items.q: (A) Looking at the crumbling frescoes, (B) the restorer (C) sighed and said (D) she wished the chapel was photographed a century earlier.
options: she wished the chapel was photographed a century earlier
items.correction: she wished the chapel had been photographed a century earlier
items.explanation: A wish about the past (a century earlier) takes the past perfect: wished the chapel had been photographed.

items.q: (A) What the astronomers (B) had failed to anticipate (C) were the amount of dust (D) the comet would shed as it neared the sun.
options: the comet would shed as it neared the sun
items.explanation: In a what-cleft the verb agrees with the singular complement the amount, so it must be was.

items.q: The nutritionist (A) suggested that (B) the school replaces (C) sugary drinks in the canteen (D) with water and unsweetened tea.
items.explanation: After suggest that, the following clause takes the base-form subjunctive (the school replace) or should replace, never the present simple -s form.

items.q: (A) Having run out of ideas, (B) the design team (C) reluctantly fell back on a sketch (D) they had earlier written out as unworkable.
options: reluctantly fell back on a sketch
they had earlier written out as unworkable
items.correction: they had earlier written off as unworkable
items.explanation: The phrasal verb meaning 'dismiss as useless' is write off; write out means to copy something in full.

items.q: (A) While waiting for the results, (B) I felt the corridor to grow longer (C) with every tick (D) of the clock above the notice board.
options: I felt the corridor to grow longer
of the clock above the notice board
items.correction: I felt the corridor grow longer
items.explanation: Verbs of perception such as feel, see and hear take object + bare infinitive (or -ing): felt the corridor grow, never to grow.

items.q: Only when (A) the last guest had left (B) did the host (C) allowed himself (D) to slump into the armchair by the fire.
options: to slump into the armchair by the fire
items.explanation: After inversion with the auxiliary did, the main verb is the bare infinitive: did the host allow himself.

items.q: (A) Despite the Alpine glaciers are retreating, (B) a handful in the Karakoram (C) appear to be holding steady, (D) puzzling climatologists.
options: Despite the Alpine glaciers are retreating,
items.correction: While the Alpine glaciers are retreating,
items.explanation: A clause of contrast with a subject and verb must be introduced by a conjunction such as While or Whereas; Despite is a preposition and takes only a noun phrase.

items.q: (A) With a view to reducing congestion, (B) the council (C) approved a cycle lane (D) in the expense of forty parking spaces.
options: With a view to reducing congestion,
in the expense of forty parking spaces
items.correction: at the expense of forty parking spaces
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is at the expense of; in does not form this idiom.

items.q: (A) Far less people than expected (B) turned up for the dawn swim, (C) partly because the forecast (D) had promised sleet.
options: turned up for the dawn swim,
items.explanation: People is a plural countable noun, so the comparative quantifier is fewer; less is reserved for uncountable nouns.
